title: Utility-scale electromagnetic delivery of power without a conductor

concept.text: The innovation would deliver utility-scale electricity across a distance using a directed electromagnetic beam. A transmitter would turn electrical input into microwave or laser energy, direct it toward a receiver, and recover electrical output at the destination. The target is sustained, useful power delivery with acceptable losses, availability and safety, rather than simply detecting a transmitted signal.

Scope synthesis: the central capability is power transmission across a gap where a line or cable is a meaningful alternative, or where a connecting conductor cannot practically be installed. Microwave and optical systems are different implementations of that capability. Electricity generation at either end, orbital infrastructure and grid integration are additional system functions; a successful beam would not by itself supply them.

significance.text: If sustained utility-scale beaming became practical, its direct significance would be logistical: electricity could reach suitable remote receivers, isolated sites or moving platforms without a connecting conductor. This could expand the options for supplying locations cut off by terrain, damaged infrastructure or operational constraints. The supplied project accounts motivate such applications, but do not demonstrate their utility-scale deployment.

Impact synthesis: the revolutionary possibility is an additional way to route substantial electrical power, not an automatic replacement for transmission networks. Ordinary corridors could continue to favor conductors wherever they offer better cost, efficiency, availability and safety. The value of a beam would depend on the application, including the infrastructure it avoids and the operating restrictions it introduces.

Space-based solar power is a conditional downstream application. Delivering collected orbital energy to Earth would require power beaming alongside launch, large-scale manufacturing, assembly, orbital transfer, durable hardware and system operation. A successful terrestrial link would not establish continuous orbital solar electricity through terrestrial night and weather, nor demonstrate that the complete orbital system is economical.

NASA's 2024 first-order assessment examined two representative space-solar-power designs normalized to 2 GW. It found baseline lifecycle electricity costs potentially about 12 to 80 times those of terrestrial renewable alternatives. More favorable scenarios combined improvements in launch, manufacturing, solar-cell efficiency, hardware lifetime and orbital transfer. These are results for the studied designs and assumptions, not a universal cost bound or proof that every possible design must achieve exactly those improvements. The supplied review supports this interpretation through the NTRS abstract and a shortened presentation, rather than the underlying complete technical study.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is the integration of sustained delivered power, useful total efficiency, reliable operation and an accepted safety case at utility scale. Existing demonstrations establish important parts of the transmission chain, but the supplied evidence does not establish that this complete capability has been achieved. It also does not establish its absence across all projects as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering synthesis from the research: a practical link must reconcile beam spreading and transmitter and receiver aperture size with pointing accuracy, receiver motion, atmospheric propagation and weather. It must also control spillover and unintended exposure. Diffraction is relevant to beam spreading, but the supplied review does not substantiate a complete quantitative aperture analysis, exposure assessment or microwave-versus-laser comparison. These remain design questions to resolve for a specified wavelength, distance, site and power level.

Atmospheric effects are an explicitly identified challenge in DARPA's optical development account. More broadly, an assessment of useful efficiency must follow energy through beam generation, propagation and conversion back to electricity. DARPA's reported optical-to-electrical efficiency covers only part of that chain, illustrating why a strong receiver result or propagation result alone cannot establish electricity-input-to-electricity-output performance.

System synthesis: scaling power also requires managing conversion losses and associated heat, maintaining beam control during interruptions or receiver movement, and demonstrating safe behavior when the intended path is obstructed or control is lost. For orbital applications, these transmission requirements sit alongside the aerospace and production challenges identified by NASA. The supplied material does not provide a complete validated engineering solution or safety analysis for these combined requirements.

current_state.text: The research attributes an X-band microwave demonstration reported in 2022 to the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory: 1.6 kW of electrical output at 1,046 m, with 73 percent radiofrequency-to-direct-current conversion at the rectenna. It also attributes to the same paper a historical comparison describing W. C. Brown's 2.39 GHz result of 34 kW received at 1.55 km as the highest earlier microwave power. These numerical claims are preserved as attributed results, but the cited paper was not captured in the supplied source record, so the review could not verify its contents, measurement boundaries or historical ranking. Even if confirmed, rectenna conversion efficiency would not establish total electricity-to-electricity efficiency.

On May 16, 2025, DARPA reported that its POWER program delivered more than 800 W during a 30-second laser transmission over 8.6 km. The same account reported efficiency above 20 percent from laser optical output to receiver electrical output at shorter distances. It did not assign that efficiency to the 8.6 km result. The demonstrated power, duration and distance therefore should be kept separate from the shorter-distance efficiency measurement, and neither measurement establishes total electrical-input-to-electrical-output efficiency.

Caltech's June 1, 2023 account reported that MAPLE powered LEDs at receivers about a foot from its transmitter in orbit. It also reported detection of a transmitted signal on a Pasadena rooftop on May 22, at the expected time and frequency and with the predicted frequency shift. These are distinct achievements: local power transfer within the orbital experiment and detection of a signal transmitted from orbit to Earth. The rooftop detection does not establish useful utility-scale electrical delivery.

NASA's 2024 material characterized space-to-ground power beaming as nascent and analyzed prospective large systems. Its modeled 2 GW designs are study scenarios, not demonstrations of operating power delivery. The available evidence described in the review consists of the substantive NTRS abstract and a complete shortened 16-page presentation; it does not include the underlying full technical study.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record establishes the dated DARPA and Caltech reports, while leaving the microwave figures unverified here. It supplies no bounded search record showing whether a later continuous megawatt demonstration existed by November 1, 2026. Consequently, it supports neither a claim that the complete capability has been achieved nor a cutoff-wide assertion that no such achievement exists. Missing evidence for the NRL paper is not evidence that its reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: demonstrate a continuous link delivering at least about one megawatt of electrical output over a distance where a line or cable is a meaningful alternative. Publish electricity-input-to-electricity-output efficiency and measure availability over weeks. This is an author-selected milestone for evaluating utility-scale progress, not an official threshold or an established industry standard.
completion_criteria.label: Continuous electrical delivery of at least about one megawatt

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: report input and delivered power, auxiliary electrical loads, losses at each conversion stage, operating conditions, interruptions and measurement uncertainty. Distinguish efficiency while transmitting from energy delivered across the full observation period, so shutdowns and weather-related interruptions remain visible. Choose and justify a quantitative efficiency acceptance threshold before the test; the supplied material does not establish one.
completion_criteria.label: Full electrical performance accounting against a predeclared efficiency acceptance threshold

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and reproducibility requirements: obtain acceptance of the safety case from the relevant regulator, document beam containment and exposure controls, and demonstrate responses to obstruction, pointing errors and loss of control. Independent verification and repeat operation under declared conditions would make the result more convincing. Tests should state the distances, weather conditions, receiver configurations and operating restrictions actually covered. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, rather than universal safety or availability.
completion_criteria.label: Regulator-accepted safety case with demonstrated controls and declared operating limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed later milestone: evaluate sustained delivery at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts before claiming consequences for bulk transmission networks. This would require application-specific comparisons of infrastructure cost, losses, availability, land or aperture requirements and safety restrictions. An orbital signal detection or a brief transmission delivering more than 800 W would not meet the proposed megawatt milestone. The earlier gigawatt, tens-to-hundreds-of-kilometers and above-80-percent figures can only be treated as possible performance ambitions; their historical provenance and authority are not established in the supplied record.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained delivery at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts evaluated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — PWR-01, Practical dissipationless conductors and windings for bulk power systems: both concepts concern delivering or handling substantial electrical power with acceptable losses. PWR-01 retains conducting paths and windings; PWR-03 transmits energy across a gap as electromagnetic radiation. Better conductors could improve equipment associated with a beam system or strengthen the competing wired option, but would not resolve beam propagation, capture or exposure requirements.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-02, Solid-state conversion of heat to utility electricity: this concerns converting thermal energy into electrical output, while PWR-03 concerns transporting energy between locations. A thermal converter could supply a transmitter, but its generation performance would remain distinct from beam-link efficiency. Neither capability establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-04, Site-independent storage from multi-day weather through seasonal imbalance: storage shifts energy across time, while PWR-03 would move it across space. Storage could buffer a receiver during beam interruptions or variations in generation. A successful beam link would not itself solve multi-day or seasonal energy imbalance, and storage would not establish long-distance beam delivery.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-05, An interconnection that no longer depends on synchronous machines: this concerns coordinated grid operation, whereas PWR-03 concerns a transmission mechanism. A utility-scale receiver would still need an electrical interface appropriate to the receiving network. Demonstrating a beam would not establish the stability, protection or control of a wider interconnection.

Space-based solar power overlaps with PWR-03 because it requires energy transfer from an orbital collection system to a receiver. It is nevertheless a broader system concept, incorporating generation, launch, assembly, lifetime and orbital operations. NASA's representative designs illustrate this added scope. Terrestrial power beaming and orbital solar power should therefore remain distinct, even where they share transmission technology.

unresolved_issues: The NRL paper's 1.6 kW output, 1,046 m distance, 73 percent rectenna efficiency, experimental duration and measurement boundaries remain unverified in the supplied evidence.
The Brown 34 kW, 1.55 km and 2.39 GHz figures, including the scope of the historical ranking, require verification from the uncaptured microwave source.
No bounded freshness search establishes whether sustained utility-scale power beaming had been demonstrated elsewhere by November 1, 2026.
The supplied DARPA account does not establish efficiency at 8.6 km, total electricity-to-electricity efficiency, or sustained availability beyond the reported 30-second transmission.
A quantitative efficiency acceptance threshold, test distance and detailed availability requirement remain to be selected for the proposed megawatt milestone.
The provenance of the earlier gigawatt, tens-to-hundreds-of-kilometers and above-80-percent performance targets is unresolved; they are not treated as official completion criteria.
The supplied evidence does not resolve the full wavelength-specific aperture, weather, exposure and regulatory trade-offs for a utility-scale implementation.
NASA's underlying complete technical study was not available in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond its abstract and shortened presentation.
The optional Caltech PDF was an unrelated institutional poster and supplies no MAPLE evidence; the relevant HTML account remains the basis for the stated experimental results.

brief.title: Large amounts of electricity delivered without wires
possible: Remote communities, isolated sites and moving vehicles could receive substantial electricity without a connecting cable. A transmitter would turn electricity into a directed beam of light or radio waves, and a receiver would turn it back into electricity.
why: This would add a way to supply places where terrain, damaged infrastructure or operating constraints make cables impractical. Its value would come from reaching receivers that are difficult to connect.

sources.showed: They modeled systems that collect sunlight in orbit and beam energy to Earth. Their baseline designs cost more than terrestrial renewable electricity; combined improvements made the modeled systems competitive.
sources.quote:
SBSP is expensive and not cost competitive with terrestrial renewable 
electricity production
sources.cited_for: Solar electricity from orbit requires improvements across the whole system, beyond power transmission.
sources.not_established: The study did not demonstrate an operating system delivering electricity from orbit.

sources.showed: This study concerns power transmission across the ground using microwaves, a form of radio wave.
sources.cited_for: It supports microwave transmission as another approach to delivering electricity without cables.
sources.not_established: Receiver conversion efficiency alone does not establish efficiency from electrical input to electrical output.

sources.who: DARPA-led team with Teravec Technologies and collaborators
sources.showed: The team delivered electricity through a brief laser transmission. Separate tests over shorter distances measured conversion from laser light to electricity.
sources.quote: Over the course of the test campaign, more than a megajoule of energy was transferred.
sources.cited_for: Laser transmission can deliver usable electrical power over substantial distances.
sources.not_established: The tests did not establish sustained operation or total efficiency from electrical input to electrical output.

sources.who: Ali Hajimiri and the Caltech team
sources.showed: Their experiment powered nearby lights in orbit. A receiver on Earth also detected a signal transmitted from the spacecraft.
sources.quote: The received signal appeared at the expected time and frequency, and had the right frequency shift as predicted based on its travel from orbit.
sources.cited_for: Power transmission equipment operated in space and directed a detectable signal toward Earth.
sources.not_established: Detecting the signal on Earth did not demonstrate delivery of useful electrical power there.

shown: DARPA’s team delivered more than 800 watts through a laser beam in a brief ground test. Caltech powered nearby lights in orbit and separately detected a signal sent to Earth. These demonstrations establish parts of the transmission chain.
missing: A practical link still needs to combine sustained substantial output, useful total efficiency and reliable operation.
Power losses and the heat they produce need to remain manageable as delivery increases.
Safety controls need to handle blocked beams, pointing errors and loss of control within accepted operating limits.

milestones.label: Continuous delivery of about a megawatt
milestones.explanation: A link would have to deliver about a megawatt continuously across a useful distance, report total electrical efficiency and measure reliability over weeks. This would test sustained delivery at a scale relevant to electricity supply.

milestones.label: Complete energy accounting meets a declared efficiency threshold
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to include all electrical loads, losses, conditions, interruptions and uncertainty, and meet an efficiency threshold chosen beforehand. This would reveal performance across the whole operating period.

milestones.label: Regulators accept demonstrated safety controls and operating limits
milestones.explanation: Regulators would have to accept controls tested against obstructions, pointing errors and control loss, with independent checks and repeated operation under declared conditions. This would establish a credible operating envelope.

milestones.label: Sustained bulk power delivery evaluated
milestones.explanation: Sustained delivery at hundreds of megawatts or more would have to be compared with cables for cost, losses, reliability, space and safety. This would test its value for major electricity networks.

uncertain: The proposed megawatt test still needs a justified efficiency threshold, distance and reliability requirement.
The balance between beam spreading, receiver size, weather and exposure limits depends on the beam and location.
Finite safety tests leave open how broadly results apply beyond the tested operating conditions.

page.title: Wireless power transmission for electricity networks
page.definition: A directed microwave or laser beam transfers power to a receiver that converts it back into electricity and supplies an electricity-network load. The operating link replaces a conducting connection between its transmitter and receiver.

goal.need: The IEA's 2026 assessment reports over 2,500 GW of renewable-generation, large-load and storage projects stalled in grid connection queues worldwide. NGED is investigating beam links for temporary connections, obstacle crossings and remote loads.

figures.caption: Infrastructure lead times reported by the IEA in 2026
figures.note: The grid range includes planning and permitting; the other ranges describe new builds.

statements.body: National Grid Electricity Distribution, WPT-for-Grid project
statements.quote: to enable quicker, more-flexible grid connections
statements.context: An Ofgem/Innovate UK Strategic Innovation Fund project.

statements.quote: Larger-scale, system-level wireless power transmission demonstrations should be planned
statements.context: Recommendation 3–4–4 in its assessment of NASA's space-solar-power investment strategy.

statements.body: DARPA, Persistent Optical Wireless Energy Relay programme
statements.quote: The program goals include demonstrating the key components necessary for a resilient, speed-of-light energy network.
statements.context: Its published final-phase objective was 10 kW of optical power reaching a ground receiver 200 km from the source laser.

completion.title: A beam link supplies an electricity-network load in operational service.
completion.criterion: An electricity-network operator uses a beam link to supply receiver-side electrical power to a network load in actual service at the WPT-for-Grid project's hundreds-of-kilowatts to low-megawatts scale. No numerical distance, efficiency, duration or availability requirement is added.
completion.basis: Searched NGED/SIF, DARPA POWER, JAXA SSPS and NASA/NRC roadmaps, plus IEC/IEEE beamed-power documents, for joint power, range, efficiency, duration and availability acceptance criteria; none was located. The fallback combines NGED's network application and power scale with TRL9's operational-proof convention. CISPR/PAS 38 concerns radio disturbances for equipment designed to operate within 10 m.

milestones.title: A beam link supplies electrical output in a laboratory validation.
milestones.criterion: Validate integrated electricity-to-beam-to-electricity transfer in a laboratory, corresponding to technology readiness level 4 (TRL4). Caltech's 2024 MAPLE paper reports ground integration tests and orbital testing of one payload beginning on 3 March 2023: two onboard receivers produced peak direct-current outputs of 231 mW and 251 mW. Its Earth experiment detected a 9.984 GHz signal.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, page 28; generic TRL4 criterion applied to the complete beam link.

milestones.title: A beam delivers more than 1 kW of electricity across more than 1 km of terrain.
milestones.criterion: Deliver >1 kW of receiver electrical output across >1 km of terrain. NRL's two-site study, published in January 2022, reports pulsed 1.6 kW output at 1,046 m, 73% receiver conversion efficiency and 1.8% efficiency from transmitter radiofrequency input to receiver electrical output. Optical progress: DARPA's 16 May 2025 release reports >800 W over 8.6 km for 30 s; >20% optical-to-electrical efficiency was measured at shorter distances. This agency report is not peer reviewed. RIT lists a related SPIE report dated 5 March 2026.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, an Operational Energy Capability Improvement Fund demonstration objective, published in Section II; written for microwaves.
milestones.threshold_quote: >1 kW of electrical power at a distance >1 km across terrain.

milestones.title: A beam link operates at hundreds of kilowatts to low megawatts with network control and safety systems.
milestones.criterion: Operate an integrated transmitter–receiver beam link at hundreds of kilowatts to low megawatts, with control and safety systems for electricity networks. This is the WPT-for-Grid development target. NGED's 2026 project page reports TRL4 hardware maturity and assessment and trial-planning outputs; it does not report operation at the target power.
milestones.set_by: NGED and Space Solar, WPT-for-Grid, funded by Ofgem/Innovate UK's Strategic Innovation Fund; written for microwave links.
milestones.threshold_quote: a high-power wireless link operating in the 100s of kW to low MW range.

milestones.title: A beam-link prototype supplies power in its intended electricity-network operating environment.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a system prototype in its intended operational environment, corresponding to TRL7. Apply the criterion to the complete beam link performing its electricity-network power-delivery function.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, page 28; generic TRL7 criterion applied to the complete beam link.
milestones.threshold_quote: system prototype demonstration in operational environment

milestones.title: The complete beam link is qualified for its intended electricity-network service.
milestones.criterion: Complete and qualify the entire beam link for its intended electricity-network service, including its transmitter, receiver and control system, corresponding to TRL8.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, page 28; generic TRL8 criterion applied to the complete beam link.

not_found: NGED's published power target does not specify an input/output measurement boundary.
Searches for 2025–2026 utility-scale beam demonstrations found no primary report establishing operational electricity-network service at the stated power scale.
The SPIE PRAD report, DOI 10.1117/12.3084832, and the DARPA-PS-25-17 solicitation text on SAM.gov could not be opened.

results.finding: One laser transmission delivered more than 800 W over 8.6 km.
results.detail: The distance exceeds 1 km, but the reported power does not establish receiver electrical output above 1 kW.
results.quote: The team recorded more than 800 watts of power delivered during a 30-second transmission from a laser 8.6 kilometers (5.3 miles) away.

results.finding: MAPLE used 2 receiver arrays to convert beamed energy to electricity and light LEDs in space.
results.detail: The source reports an integrated space demonstration and says MAPLE was tested on Earth, but does not describe an integrated laboratory validation.
results.quote: MAPLE features two separate receiver arrays located about a foot away from the transmitter to receive the energy, convert it to direct current (DC) electricity, and use it to light up a pair of LEDs to demonstrate the full sequence of wireless energy transmission at a distance in space.

results.finding: Microwave power transmission tests, sample size not stated, achieved 54% overall DC-to-DC efficiency.
results.detail: The report describes integrated DC-to-microwave-to-DC transfer, but the supplied text does not state that the certified tests took place in a laboratory or establish TRL 4.
results.quote: The procedures and the hardware developed were the basis for tests certified by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in which an overall dc to dc efficiency of 54 percent was achieved.

results.finding: One microwave receiver array delivered over 30 kW of DC output across 1.54 km.
results.detail: The receiver supplied lamp and resistor loads at a Mojave Desert test site. This is a technical memorandum reporting the authors’ own experiment.
results.quote:
Over 30 kW of DC output power has been transmitted a distance of
1.54 km without wires.

results.finding: One microwave beam-link test produced up to 30.4 kW of DC output.
results.detail: The integrated link operated at an outdoor test range; the reported experiment was not a laboratory validation.
results.quote:
Incident peak RF intensities of up to 170 mW/cm 2 have yielded
up to 30.4 kW of DC output power.

results.finding: One microwave beam-link test produced up to 30.4 kW of DC output.
results.detail: The test included monitoring and automatic shutdown provisions, but its reported DC output was below the hundreds-of-kilowatts criterion, and it did not demonstrate electricity-network controls and safety systems.
results.quote:
Incident peak RF intensities of up to 170 mW/cm 2 have yielded
up to 30.4 kW of DC output power.

results.finding: MAPLE: one payload delivered a peak 251 mW of rectified DC power to its broadside receiver in orbit.
results.detail: Six pre-launch ground integration tests measured rectified receiver power. The reported 251 mW peak was achieved in orbit; the separate beam-to-Earth experiment detected a signal rather than supplying a load.
results.quote:
The peak rectified DC powers received by the sidewall and broad-
side rectennas were 231 mW and 251 mW, respectively.

results.finding: Star Catcher laser tests, number of tests unspecified: more than 1.1 kW of electrical power delivered.
results.detail: The release does not state the transmission distance, so it does not establish delivery across more than 1 km.
results.quote: Using an advanced suite of multi-wavelength lasers, the team delivered more than 1.1 kW of electrical power to commercial off-the-shelf solar panels at Space Florida’s Launch and Landing Facility.

results.finding: Star Catcher laser demonstration (n=1) reportedly beamed over 1 kW over a kilometer.
results.detail: The source does not specify whether the power was receiver electrical output, as required by the criterion.
results.quote: Over a kilowatt of power over a kilometer and distance.
